findings: A: killed by "how many blows take it to a hundred millimetres" against "The floor is 130 millimetres of washed silica sand" — the count stops at 100 mm, 30 mm short of the bottom of the bed.
B: killed by "under a ring weight raised to a collar and let fall" — the collar fixes the drop height; it is not varied point by point.
C: confirmed by "in the cold the first blow took the cone two-thirds as deep, and the count nearly doubled" — two-thirds of a depth is shallower, and a near-doubled count is higher.
D: killed by "The gap between my February morning and my July afternoon is still wider than the gap between this school and any other school I test" — the option reverses the stated ordering.
justification: Arithmetic check: cold first-blow depth = 2/3 of warm (ratio 0.67 < 1, i.e. shallower) and cold count = about 2x warm (higher). Both halves of C reconcile with the one sentence that reports the two figures. D is the same comparison inverted, so exactly one of C and D can stand; the text fixes which.

findings: A: killed by "the wax he brought up from the bottom was in better condition than the wax at the top" — the lower wax is the better-preserved wax, not worn off.
B: killed by "the grains he sieved came out much as the original specification had them" — the sand is unchanged against spec.

C: killed by "Eighty millimetres of it had not been turned since the day it was laid, and under nine years of hoofprints it had gone firm enough to lean a spade on" — below the tines the bed is hard, not loose.
D: confirmed by "In the top 50 millimetres the fibre came out at about 8 per cent by weight; lower down it was nearer 3."
justification: Ratio check: 8 per cent by weight in the top 50 mm against about 3 per cent below, a factor of roughly 2.7, which supports much less fibre at the bottom. The figures also reconcile with the mechanism given, since harrowing to only 50 mm on a 130 mm bed lifts fibre into the top 50 mm and leaves 80 mm starved of it.

findings: A: killed by "The waxed ones move, whatever their age" together with "some of them older than this one" — age is explicitly ruled out as the variable, and the sprinklered schools are never said to be newer.

B: confirmed by "In the schools laid on plain sand and fibre and kept damp with a sprinkler, the morning grid and the afternoon grid sit almost on top of one another" read with "The wax is a paraffin blend, and it is doing most of that work" — plain sand and fibre is sand without the wax coating, and the wax is what the daily movement is attributed to.

C: killed by "laid over a membrane and crushed stone" — this school has a membrane too and still moves, so a membrane cannot be what steadies the sprinklered ones; nothing in the text ties a membrane to holding water.

D: killed by "He has the same pair of grids from a hundred and forty other arenas" against "He read a grid of thirty points at seven" and "the same grid at four" — the other arenas are read on the same morning-and-afternoon pair, not at a different hour.
justification: The comparison class is defined by two properties at once, no wax and a sprinkler, so the wax attribution has to come from elsewhere in the text; it does, from the paraffin mechanism and from the claim that the waxed ones move whatever their age. Confidence is held below 0.9 only because the sprinkler is an uncontrolled co-variate in that one sentence; no option exploits it, so B stands alone.

findings: A: confirmed by "Here Pallenmoor is careful, and the care is the most useful thing about him" and by "That is a good deal less than the trade’s brochures offer, and it is worth more than they are."
B: killed by "The tester measures a surface; there is no horse above the cone" — the soundness question is left open, so the tine change cannot be read as an answer to it.
C: killed by "Both figures moved, and they moved together" — the readings confirm the riders; what they correct is "The yard has blamed the machine, then the mix, then the man on the tractor."

D: killed by "That is a good deal less than the trade’s brochures offer, and it is worth more than they are" — the brochures offer more and are rated worth less, which is the opposite of the position D attributes to her.
justification: D is the nearest miss because the brochures do literally offer more; but the stem asks for the position the writer takes, and her stated valuation puts the fuller claim below the careful one. A names exactly the thing she calls the most useful.

findings: A: killed by "Below about six degrees the coating is stiff, the grains lock together" — the locking is the paraffin stiffening, not ice, and the cold reading was taken "with the school at three degrees", above freezing, with no water mentioned in the bed.

B: killed on the two stated thresholds: "Below about six degrees the coating is stiff" and "Above about twenty-five it goes slack". Heating lifts a February school clear of the 6 degree floor but not to the July afternoon that the riders call "deep and tiring by a July afternoon", i.e. above 25. The text also never pairs a warm February with July: the only comparison offered is "The gap between my February morning and my July afternoon".

C: confirmed by "The temperature is doing more in that room than the tractor is" together with "so the machine had been slowly sorting the bed into a loose layer riding on a hard one" and the closing frame "The yard has changed one thing and left the other alone" — the piece identifies exactly two levers, room temperature and how deep the tines run.
D: killed by "The temperature is doing more in that room than the tractor is" — D reverses the ranking the tester gives.
justification: FLAG, not kill: B is the closest thing in the batch to a second defensible reading, and a strong candidate who reads temperature as the whole story could choose it. It is killed on an explicit threshold argument rather than on a flat contradiction: the wax has two regimes, below about 6 and above about 25, so warming February out of the stiff regime does not put it in July's slack regime, and no reading in the text pairs a warm February with a July afternoon. Reviewers should confirm they are content with a key that needs that two-threshold step to separate C from B.

findings: A: killed by "and again there has been no signal" — the unanimous ending is a second instance of the same puzzle, not a consequence of the unanimous start, so a resultative connective does not fit.
B: killed by "the ending is unanimous" — nothing in the preceding sentence is being corrected or replaced, so a corrective connective has nothing to work against.

C: confirmed by the parallel between "two hundred people find the same half-second" and "the ending is unanimous: five seconds later the sound stops, and again there has been no signal" — a likewise connective is what the parallel requires.
D: killed by "The clapping in the school hall" — the second observation is made in the same hall, not in another place.
justification: The gap sits between two statements of the same phenomenon at opposite ends of the applause; the word has to mark addition of a like case.

findings: A: confirmed by "for the length of one clap you are alone with an opinion nobody asked for" — the risk is that nobody else participates, which is what the join-in phrasal verb names.
B: killed by the same span — an interrupting sense would not produce being alone; the room is failing to take part, not failing to interrupt.
C: killed by "there is no conductor to watch" — a falling-in sense implies following a lead that the text says is absent.
D: killed by "The risk of putting your hands together in a quiet room" — a breaking-in sense describes an intrusion, not the room declining to participate.
justification: Collocation and sense agree on the participation reading; the clause after the gap supplies the test.

findings: A: killed by "conducted at speed and without words" — the head noun is something carried on over time; a transaction is an exchange, and nothing is being exchanged here.

B: confirmed by "the coming-down is a" plus "about how long is decent, conducted at speed and without words" — a negotiation is the process noun that takes both the about-complement and the conducted verb.
C: killed by "conducted at speed and without words" — a bargain is the outcome that is struck, not the wordless process being conducted.
D: killed by the same span — a settlement likewise names the result reached, whereas the sentence describes the working-out itself, "the sound comes down faster than it went up".
justification: All four are near-synonyms in the same field, so the gap turns on which of them is a process rather than an outcome and which takes conducted. Only the process noun satisfies both.

findings: A: killed by "No one has agreed to anything, there is no conductor to watch" — the whole piece insists the applause is unprepared.
B: killed by "conducted at speed and without words" — applause has no words, so an outspoken quality cannot be predicated of it.

C: killed by the concessive frame "Although what a hall gives an eight-year-old is ___(4)___, it is not permitted to run long" — a brevity word makes the concession self-cancelling, since brief and not long agree rather than contrast.
D: confirmed by the same concessive frame against "Four or five seconds, then a ragged tail" — warmth that is nonetheless capped at four or five seconds is exactly the contrast the although demands.
justification: The gap is fixed by the concessive: the filler must be a quality that would otherwise argue for a long clap. Only the wholehearted reading does that, and C fails precisely because it agrees with the main clause instead of opposing it.

findings: A: killed by "A room asked for a big hand for a stranger will give one" — a narrowly reading has no scale here to be narrow on.

B: confirmed by "and everybody present can hear that it is not the same sound the recorder player got" — the applause is given because it was asked for and is audibly less warm, which is the dutiful reading.
C: killed by "A room asked for a big hand" — being asked is the opposite of instinctive; the instinctive case in this text is the unprompted hall that "organises itself in about a fifth of a second".
D: killed by "it is not the same sound the recorder player got" — an eager reading would make it the warmer sound, not the lesser one.
justification: The second clause grades the applause as audibly inferior to the genuine article, which rules out both enthusiasm words and leaves the obligation word.

findings: A: confirmed by "It’s the stop at the far end that does it" against "Between stations the shocks were tiny" — the damage is localised to the arrival stop.
B: killed by "Nothing shows on the ward; the colour comes with the spinning" — the pink is only visible after centrifugation in the lab.
C: killed by "Blood gases have never gone by tube; a porter walks those down" — blood gases are the one thing that does not go by tube.
D: killed by "The loop runs at the speed it always has" — the halved reject rate follows "Two bins are lined with foam", not any change of speed.
justification: Every distractor is a single inverted fact from the passage, and each inversion has an explicit sentence against it. A restates the attributed cause verbatim.

findings: A: killed by "The neighbour’s attorney enclosed a tracing of the railway company’s deposited plan" — the plan is brought into the correspondence by the neighbour himself.

B: killed by "cut from above by one and cleaned from below by the other" against "both sides agree the thorn was last laid in 1839" — the bank was being maintained, and a six-year interval since the last laying is an ordinary point in a laying cycle, not neglect; the text gives no complaint about the hedge itself.

C: killed on the dates: the claim is made "In November 1845", and "The previous October a surveyor had chained and pegged the line along the bank", i.e. October 1845, one month before the attorneys begin. The pluperfect confirms the ordering.

D: confirmed by matching "the bank, the ditch and the timber from the stone gap down to the lane" to "chained and pegged the line along the bank, from the ash to the culvert" through "An ash grew in the stone gap; a culvert ran under the lane" — the two descriptions name the same stretch by two sets of landmarks.
justification: Date arithmetic: surveyor October 1845, claim November 1845, letters to March 1846, offer February 1846, scheme abandoned autumn 1846, joint laying 1851. The sequence reconciles and puts the pegging one month before the claim, which both kills C and supplies the motive that makes D the implication. The endpoint identity is exact once the ash is read as the stone-gap tree and the culvert as the lane crossing.

findings: A: bekräftas av "Från och med nästa spelår bör texten gå på varje föreställning på stora scenen, inte på fyra utvalda." och av att hon godtar kostnaden: "Så lyder ensemblens invändning, och jag skriver under på den." samt "Ändå ska den bäras."
B: faller på "Ett svepskäl är det inte." — hon avvisar uttryckligen att invändningen skulle dölja något annat.

C: faller på "Fler särskilda kvällar begär jag inte." och på "Att ensemblen vänjer sig vid remsan kan jag inte lova." — hon vill inte ha fler utvalda kvällar och gör ingen takt beroende av tillvänjning.
D: faller på "och något förslag för den scenen har jag inte" — hon lämnar uttryckligen lilla scenen utan förslag.
justification: Stycket Ändå ska den bäras binder ihop de två halvorna av A: hon erkänner att spelet binds hårdare vid manus och kräver ändå textning på varje föreställning på stora scenen. De tre övriga motsägs var för sig av en explicit mening.

findings: A: faller på "Slingans symbol finns längst ned på varje uppslag i programbladet och har gjort det i alla år." — symbolen hör till uppslaget, inte till raden.
B: faller på samma mening — det som upprepas längst ned på varje uppslag är slingans symbol, inte raden.
C: faller på "Längre bak i programbladet står Ingegerd Hörnfeldt under rubriken Text och teknik." — namnet står längre bak, inte på raden.
D: bekräftas av "inklämd mellan syntolkning och skolföreställningar".
justification: Frågan gäller enbart raden i höstprogrammet. Två distraktorer flyttar över egenskaper från slingsymbolen och en från personsidan längre bak; bara D beskriver raden.

findings.span: Skaren som bar en karl gick sönder under hoven
findings.note: Direkt stöd: skaren som bar en gående karl brast under hoven, dvs. hovarna sjönk igenom där folk gick. Förstärks av ett djur som trampade igenom skar upp benen på iskanten.

findings.span: mot det hjälper varken broddar eller lättare lass
findings.note: Texten säger uttryckligen att broddar inte hjälper mot hovtrycket; B påstår motsatsen.

findings.span: Lassen gick på kälke i stället, och kälken drogs för hand.
findings.note: Kälken drogs för hand, inte av häst; C flyttar dragarbetet tillbaka till hästen.

Att hästen fick stå i stallet är oförenligt med att den användes till annat. Caveat: texten uttalar sig bara om att hästen hölls utanför skarkörningen och är tyst om eventuell annan sysselsättning under resten av de veckorna; dödandet vilar alltså på ett litet slutledningssteg plus total avsaknad av stöd, inte på en punktvis motsägelse.

justification: Stycket om hästen ger ett entydigt svar: skaren som bar en karl brast under hoven eftersom en hov samlar hela tyngden på en tallriksstor yta. A är den enda formulering som återger detta. B motsägs ordagrant (broddar hjälper inte), C motsägs av att kälken drogs för hand, och D är oförenlig med att hästen fick stå i stallet. Inget annat alternativ går att försvara på texten.

findings.span: Man såg på himlen och bestämde sig kvällen innan.
findings.note: Stöds av Veckorna kom när de kom. och Somliga år blev det fyra morgnar på hela vintern, och ett par vintrar uteblev skaren. Friktion: att besluta kvällen innan är i strikt mening ett beslut i förväg; nyckeln kräver läsningen att i förväg avser planering längre fram än kvällen före. Kontexten (vädret avgör, veckorna kom när de kom) gör den läsningen klart rimligast, men lexikal friktion finns.

findings.span: Var gård körde för sig, och sällan väntade någon in grannen.
findings.note: Varje gård körde för sig och väntade sällan in grannen; det utesluter både turtagning och delat slit.

findings.span: Skidor dög till att ta sig fram med, men inte till att dra med.
findings.note: Uttrycklig motsägelse: skidor dög inte till att dra med. Lassen gick på kälke i stället, och kälken drogs för hand.

findings.span: Ett lass som inte är hemma vid tio blir liggande till nästa natt.
findings.note: Körningen slutade med bärigheten (vid tio är det över), inte när sista lasset var hemma; ett lass som inte hann hem blev liggande.

justification: Frågan gäller hur arbetet lades upp. A, C och D motsägs var för sig av en explicit mening i texten (var gård för sig; skidor dög inte till att dra med; lass som inte är hemma vid tio blir liggande). Kvar står B, som stöds av att veckorna kom när de kom, att skaren somliga vintrar uteblev helt, och att man såg på himlen och bestämde sig först kvällen innan. B är därmed enda försvarbara alternativ. Sänkt konfidens enbart för den lexikala friktionen mellan i förväg och bestämde sig kvällen innan; ingen andra försvarbar nyckel uppstår ur den friktionen, så item är svarbart.
